newsitem.title: ITALY: MOTOR RACING-SENNA MANSLAUGHTER TRIAL OPENS.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-SENNA MANSLAUGHTER TRIAL OPENS.

text.p: Frederico Bendinelli, managing director of the Imola track, was the only defendant present on the opening day on Thursday at the trial of six men charged with manslaughter over the death of Ayrton Senna.
Formula One team chief Frank Williams and five others have been accused of manslaughter after Brazilian three times world champion Senna died at the San Marino Grand Prix on May 1, 1994.
The defendants, who include Patrick Head, technical director of the Williams team and designer Adrian Newey, deny responsibility for the fatal crash.

Court president Antonio Costanzo opened the session, which is due to focus on legal preliminaries, and retired after 15 minutes to decide if the television crews and photographers would be allowed at future hearings.
The high-profile trial is taking palce in a dance hall specially converted for the occasion, its disco lights and sound system still on the walls.
Near them are a sign reading `The law is the same for everyone` and a crucifix, two staples of Italian courtrooms.
Bendinelli said the circuit was not responsible for Senna's death.
"I am completely calm and convinced that no responsibility will be laid at the circuit's door," he said.
"It seemed there was a curse on the 1994 Grand Prix. We saw things there that had never been witnessed in any other (motor racing) championship in the world," he said.
The case has sent shock waves through Formula One. Teams have warned they will not risk competing in Italy in the event of a guilty verdict.
"I hope that the trial will end with the acquittal of all the defendants," Bendinelli added.
After Thursday's session, the trial is due to be adjourned until February 28. First witnesses are due to be heard next month and Williams is not due to appear until April.

Senna suffered fatal head injuries when his Williams hurtled into a concrete wall at around 220 kph during the race. Italian state prosecutors believe that the steering column on the Brazilian's car snapped as a result of poor welding.
The case is scheduled to last three months but one legal source close to Williams said he did not foresee a verdict until the autumn.
